Ethiopia
ē-thĭ-ō'pĭ-ă
n. (the KJV rendering of Cush, the land south of Egypt — the far country of Scripture, and the first Gentile convert of the book of Acts)
The KJV renders Hebrew Kush as Ethiopia after the Greek Aithiopia, from aitho, to burn, and ops, face — the land of the sun-darkened. Cush is a son of Ham (Gen 10:6), and the biblical Cush lies along the upper Nile, in modern Sudan rather than the modern Ethiopian state.

Biblical Definition

Ethiopia in the KJV translates the Hebrew Cush, the land beyond the southern border of Egypt, and it functions in Scripture as the far country — the edge of the known world. It appears at the beginning, where Gihon “compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia” (Gen 2:13); Moses married an Ethiopian woman and Miriam was struck leprous for despising it; Ebedmelech the Ethiopian eunuch pulled Jeremiah out of the dungeon with old rags for his armpits, an act of mercy God rewarded by name. Jeremiah also coins the proverb of the unchangeable heart: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23) — a text on total depravity, not on complexion. Above all there is the psalm: “Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God” (Psa 68:31). Luke records the answer. Philip is sent to a desert road to meet “a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians” (Act 8:27), reading Isaiah 53 in a chariot. He was baptised and went on his way rejoicing, and the far country had stretched out its hands.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives Ethiopia as a country of Africa south of Egypt, and Ethiopian as its inhabitant, noting the Greek derivation from a burnt or sun-blackened countenance.

expand to see more

ETHIOPIA, n. A country of Africa lying south of Egypt, called in Hebrew Cush.

The name is Greek, and denotes the country of the sun-burnt visage.

ETHIOPIAN, n. A native of Ethiopia; a blackamoor.

Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a servant in the house of the king of Judah, delivered Jeremiah from the dungeon.

An eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, was baptized by Philip the evangelist.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:13 — "And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia."

Psa 68:31 — "Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God."

Jer 13:23 — "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil."

Act 8:27 — "And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship,"

Modern Corruption

Jer 13:23 has been abused in both directions — quoted to demean, and then avoided out of embarrassment; its actual subject is the bondage of the will, and the whole Reformed doctrine of depravity is in it.

expand to see more

“Can the Ethiopian change his skin” has a shameful history of misuse in Western Christendom, cited to suggest a permanent defect in a people. The verse says the opposite of what the abusers made of it. The point of comparison is not that the skin is bad but that it is unalterable by the man who wears it — and that is the prophet's picture of Judah's heart, not of Cush. The whole force of the analogy depends on the Ethiopian and the leopard being simply what God made them. Anyone who reads a slur into it has inverted the grammar. The dictionary holds Gen 1:27 without qualification: every human being of every nation is an image-bearer, and Act 17:26 makes all nations of one blood.

The doctrine the verse actually teaches is the one modern preaching most avoids: the sinner's inability. Not that the wicked will not do good, but that they cannot — “accustomed to do evil” renders a word for the learned habit that has become a nature. This is the bondage of the will that Luther defended against Erasmus and that the 1689 Confession states in chapter nine: fallen man has “wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good.” A gospel offered to people who merely need better motivation is a different gospel. The Ethiopian in Act 8 did not change his own heart either; he was sent a preacher.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Kush (H3568), Cush, rendered Ethiopia; Greek Aithiops (G128), Ethiopian; eunouchos (G2135), a eunuch.

expand to see more

Hebrew Kush (H3568) — Cush, son of Ham (Gen 10:6) and the land of his posterity above Egypt.

Hebrew Kushi (H3569) — a Cushite, Ethiopian; the word used of Ebedmelech and of Moses' wife.

Greek Aithiops (G128) — Ethiopian; used only of the eunuch in Act 8.

Greek eunouchos (G2135) — a eunuch; barred from the congregation under the law (Deu 23:1), and promised a name better than of sons (Isa 56:5).

Hebrew Kandake / Greek Kandake (G2582) — Candace, a dynastic title of the queens of Meroe, not a personal name.

Usage

"“Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God” — the psalm Act 8 answers."

"“Can the Ethiopian change his skin” — the proverb of a will in bondage."

"“A man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority” — the far country come to Isaiah 53."
